issue.body:
### Description

I was surprised to discover that `vmap` does not always convert NumPy arrays into JAX arrays. Instead, it sometimes (rarely) will return NumPy arrays when given NumPy arrays as inputs:
```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

numpy_array = np.arange(3)
print(type(jax.vmap(lambda x: x)(numpy_array)))  # <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
print(type(jax.vmap(jnp.asarray)(numpy_array)))  # <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
print(type(jax.vmap(jnp.array)(numpy_array)))  # <class 'jaxlib.xla_extension.ArrayImpl'>
```

The exceptions appear to be cases where the wrapped function is evaluated to the "identity", as least as far as JAXprs are concerned:
```python
print(jax.make_jaxpr(jax.vmap(jnp.asarray))(jax_array))
# { lambda ; a:i32[3]. let  in (a,) }
```

However, `jnp.asarray()` is also explicitly converting inputs into a JAX arrays, so I found this doubly surprsing.

My real-use is a custom pytree type where the constructor (but not `tree_unflatten`) always converts inputs into JAX arrays, which otherwise seems perfectly well behaved and is one of the [suggested patterns](https://jax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pytrees.html#custom-pytrees-and-initialization) in the JAX docs. `vmap` returns an otherwise impossible to create value when applied to this "identity function":
```python
@jax.tree_util.register_pytree_node_class
class Wrapper:
  def __init__(self, value):
    self.value = jnp.asarray(value)

  def tree_flatten(self):
    return [self.value], None
  
  @classmethod
  def tree_unflatten(cls, _, leaves):
    result = super().__new__(cls)
    [result.value] = leaves
    return result

  def __repr__(self):
    return f"Wrapped({self.value!r})"


print(type(jax.vmap(Wrapper)(np.arange(3)).value))
# <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
```

### System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.)

jaxlib: 0.4.38
numpy:  1.26.4

issue.body:
Fixes #14921

One reason for this is so that we can potentially add an `asarray` primitive without adding that to the trace of all our APIs (related to #25745 and #18020)

Another reason for this is that by avoiding internal calls to `jnp.asarray`, this change leads to improved trace-time, by close to ~50% in some cases (related to #25931).

Using 100 applications of `jnp.flip` as a simple benchmark...

Timing on the main branch:
```python
In [1]: import jax.numpy as jnp

In [2]: import jax

In [3]: def f(x):
   ...:     for i in range(100):
   ...:         x = jnp.flip(x)
   ...:     return x
   ...: 

In [4]: %timeit jax.eval_shape(lambda x: f(x), jnp.arange(10))
4.39 ms ± 16.6 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```
Timing on this branch
```python
In [1]: import jax.numpy as jnp

In [2]: import jax

In [3]: def f(x):
   ...:     for i in range(100):
   ...:         x = jnp.flip(x)
   ...:     return x
   ...: 

In [4]: %timeit jax.eval_shape(lambda x: f(x), jnp.arange(10))
2.36 ms ± 1.97 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```
There are still a number of other places where this new helper could be applied, but I'm going to limit it to `lax_numpy.py` for the first set of changes.

issue.body:
This is an experiment toward a fix to #25745 and #18020.

Basically, we currently lower `jnp.asarray` to nothing in many cases, and this leads to strange behavior under some transformations; for example:
```python
In [1]: import jax

In [2]: import numpy as np

In [3]: out = jax.vmap(jax.numpy.asarray)(np.arange(4))

In [4]: type(out)
Out[4]: numpy.ndarray
```
The fix here ensures that `asarray` lowers to a primitive, so that these kinds of corner cases behave as expected.

Many of the test failures here should be fixed by work related to #25931, which removes calls to `jnp.asarray` from JAX API implementations.
